claim: AIM-100 promotes dramatic oligomerization, clustering and clathrin-independent endocytosis of human and mouse dopamine transporters (DAT).
source: We found that the cell-permeable furopyrimidine AIM-100 promotes dramatic oligomerization, clustering and CIE of human and mouse dopamine transporters (DAT), but not of their close homologues, norepinephrine and serotonin transporters.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1-4 showing oligomerization, clustering, and endocytosis of DAT in response to AIM-100 treatment.

claim: AIM-100 does not promote oligomerization, clustering and endocytosis of norepinephrine and serotonin transporters.
source: We found that the cell-permeable furopyrimidine AIM-100 promotes dramatic oligomerization, clustering and CIE of human and mouse dopamine transporters (DAT), but not of their close homologues, norepinephrine and serotonin transporters.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing that AIM-100 does not induce clustering/endocytosis of NET or SERT.

claim: All effects of AIM-100 on DAT and the occupancy of substrate binding sites in the transporter are mutually exclusive.
source: All effects of AIM-100 on DAT and the occupancy of substrate binding sites in the transporter were mutually exclusive, suggesting that AIM-100 may act by binding to DAT.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 5-6 showing that cocaine, dopamine, amphetamine, and modafinil inhibit AIM-100 effects on DAT.

claim: AIM-100 may act by binding to DAT.
source: All effects of AIM-100 on DAT and the occupancy of substrate binding sites in the transporter were mutually exclusive, suggesting that AIM-100 may act by binding to DAT.
evidence: Inferred from mutual exclusivity of AIM-100 effects and substrate binding, and from previous studies showing AIM-100 inhibits cocaine analog binding.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis is independent of dynamin.
source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis was independent of dynamin, cholesterol-rich microdomains and actin cytoskeleton, implying that a novel endocytic mechanism is involved.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 11A showing dynamin-2 knockdown does not inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis is independent of cholesterol-rich microdomains.
source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis was independent of dynamin, cholesterol-rich microdomains and actin cytoskeleton, implying that a novel endocytic mechanism is involved.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 11B showing nystatin (cholesterol-chelating drug) does not inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis is independent of actin cytoskeleton.
source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis was independent of dynamin, cholesterol-rich microdomains and actin cytoskeleton, implying that a novel endocytic mechanism is involved.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 11B showing Latranculin B (actin inhibitor) does not inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.

claim: A novel endocytic mechanism is involved in AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis was independent of dynamin, cholesterol-rich microdomains and actin cytoskeleton, implying that a novel endocytic mechanism is involved.
evidence: Inferred from the independence of AIM-100-induced endocytosis from multiple known endocytic mechanisms.

claim: AIM-100 stimulated trafficking of internalized DAT results in accumulation in early endosomes without significant recycling or degradation.
source: AIM-100 stimulated trafficking of internalized DAT was also unusual: DAT accumulated in early endosomes without significant recycling or degradation.
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 7-9 showing DAT colocalization with early endosome markers and lack of recycling or degradation.

claim: AIM-100 augments DAT oligomerization through an allosteric mechanism associated with the DAT conformational state.
source: We propose that AIM-100 augments DAT oligomerization through an allosteric mechanism associated with the DAT conformational state, and that oligomerization-triggered clustering leads to a coat-independent endocytosis and subsequent endosomal retention of DAT.
evidence: Proposed based on non-competitive inhibition of CFT binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and effects of conformational state modulators (Figures 5-6).

claim: Oligomerization-triggered clustering leads to a coat-independent endocytosis and subsequent endosomal retention of DAT.
source: We propose that AIM-100 augments DAT oligomerization through an allosteric mechanism associated with the DAT conformational state, and that oligomerization-triggered clustering leads to a coat-independent endocytosis and subsequent endosomal retention of DAT.
evidence: Proposed based on correlation between oligomerization, clustering, and endocytosis, and independence from known coat proteins.

claim: Treatment of PAE cells stably expressing YFP-HA-DAT with AIM-100 at 37°C resulted in dramatic re-distribution of YFP-HA-DAT from the plasma membrane to intracellular vesicular compartments.
source: Direct YFP imaging demonstrated that treatment of porcine aortic endothelial (PAE) cells stably expressing YFP-HA-DAT with AIM-100 at 37°C resulted in dramatic re-distribution of YFP-HA-DAT from the plasma membrane, where the transporter is concentrated in filopodia, cell edges and ruffles, to intracellular vesicular compartments (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly observed in microscopy images shown in Figure 1A.

claim: AIM-100-induced vesicular accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT was observed at AIM-100 concentrations ≥ 10 µM and reached a maximal extent at 20 µM.
source: AIM-100-induced vesicular accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT was observed at AIM-100 concentrations ≥ 10 µM and reached a maximal extent at 20 µM (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by dose-response imaging in Figure 1B.

claim: AIM-100-induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis follows linear kinetics without reaching a plateau for at least 2 hr.
source: Quantitative analysis of the time-course of YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis induced by AIM-100 using an HA antibody uptake assay revealed that this endocytosis follows a linear kinetics without reaching a plateau for at least 2 hr (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Demonstrated by time-course measurements in Figure 1C-D showing linear relationship (R2=0.9693).

claim: Linear kinetics of AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis is characteristic of a non-saturable and/or irreversible trafficking process.
source: Such kinetics is characteristic of a non-saturable and/or irreversible trafficking process.
evidence: Inferred from the observed linear kinetics pattern.

claim: Cell-surface biotinylation experiments confirmed down-regulation of the plasma membrane YPF-HA-DAT by approximately 75% after a 2 hr AIM-100 treatment of PAE cells.
source: Cell-surface biotinylation experiments confirmed down-regulation of the plasma membrane YPF-HA-DAT by approximately 75% after a 2 hr AIM-100 treatment of PAE cells (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Quantified from biotinylation experiments shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: AIM-100 treatment results in a greater than 5-fold increase in the fraction of high molecular mass species (~290 kDa) of YFP-HA-DAT in lysates of PAE cells.
source: Surprisingly, a greater than 5-fold increase in the fraction of high molecular mass species (~290 kDa) of YFP-HA-DAT was observed in lysates of AIM-100-treated cells when compared with vehicle-treated cells (Figure 1E and G).
evidence: Quantified from Western blot analysis in Figure 1E and G.

claim: A discrete band of a high molecular mass DAT species can be detected in the absence of AIM-100, although the relative fraction of this species (10–40%) varies between different experiments and between cell lines.
source: The same, discrete band of a high molecular mass DAT species could also be detected consistently in the absence of AIM-100, although the relative fraction of this species (10–40%) varies between different experiments and between cell lines.
evidence: Observed in Western blot experiments across multiple figures.

claim: AIM-100 substantially increases the amount of high molecular mass DAT species and the abundance of larger DAT species, suggesting that AIM-100 stabilizes SDS-resistant DAT oligomers and higher-order oligomers.
source: AIM-100 substantially increased the amount of this species, and in addition, the abundance of the larger DAT species in all experiments, suggesting that AIM-100 stabilizes SDS-resistant DAT oligomers and higher-order oligomers.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot data showing increased oligomeric species with AIM-100 treatment.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT oligomers are not disrupted by β-mercaptoethanol, iodoacetamide, or dithiothreitol (DTT).
source: Because AIM-100-induced oligomers were not disrupted by β-mercaptoethanol, iodoacetamide (see 'Methods') and dithiothreitol (DTT) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), oligomerization was not due to formation of disulfide bonds between DAT molecules.
evidence: Demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization is not due to formation of disulfide bonds between DAT molecules.
source: Because AIM-100-induced oligomers were not disrupted by β-mercaptoethanol, iodoacetamide (see 'Methods') and dithiothreitol (DTT) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), oligomerization was not due to formation of disulfide bonds between DAT molecules.
evidence: Inferred from resistance to reducing agents shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ratio of oligomers to monomers (O/M) in the biotinylated fraction was significantly increased by AIM-100 demonstrating that AIM-100 induces DAT oligomerization at the cell surface.
source: The ratio of oligomers to monomers (O/M) in the biotinylated fraction was significantly increased by AIM-100 demonstrating that AIM-100 induces DAT oligomerization at the cell surface (Figure 1G).
evidence: Quantified from biotinylation experiments in Figure 1G.

claim: The O/M ratio was 4-times lower in the biotinylated fraction than in total cell lysates (surface plus endosomal DAT) in AIM-100-treated cells.
source: However, the O/M ratio was 4-times lower in the biotinylated fraction than in total cell lysates (surface plus endosomal DAT) in AIM-100-treated cells.
evidence: Calculated from data in Figure 1G comparing biotinylated and total lysate fractions.

claim: AIM-100-induced DAT oligomers are enriched in endosomes as compared to the plasma membrane.
source: This data indicate that AIM-100-induced DAT oligomers are enriched in endosomes as compared to the plasma membrane, and suggest that oligomerization facilitates DAT endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in O/M ratios between biotinylated (surface) and total (surface + endosomal) fractions.

claim: Oligomerization facilitates DAT endocytosis.
source: This data indicate that AIM-100-induced DAT oligomers are enriched in endosomes as compared to the plasma membrane, and suggest that oligomerization facilitates DAT endocytosis.
evidence: Suggested based on enrichment of oligomers in endosomes.

claim: Small amounts of immature monomeric (~70 kDa) and corresponding oligomeric YFP-HA-DAT (~200 kDa) were detected in lysates of untreated and AIM-100-treated cells, respectively, but not in the biotinylated fractions.
source: Small amounts of immature monomeric (~70 kDa) and corresponding oligomeric YFP-HA-DAT (~200 kDa) were detected in lysates of untreated and AIM-100-treated cells, respectively, but not in the biotinylated fractions (Figure 1E), indicating that AIM-100 also causes oligomerization of newly-synthesized DAT located in the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: Observed in Western blots in Figure 1E.

claim: AIM-100 causes oligomerization of newly-synthesized DAT located in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Small amounts of immature monomeric (~70 kDa) and corresponding oligomeric YFP-HA-DAT (~200 kDa) were detected in lysates of untreated and AIM-100-treated cells, respectively, but not in the biotinylated fractions (Figure 1E), indicating that AIM-100 also causes oligomerization of newly-synthesized DAT located in the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence: Inferred from detection of immature oligomers in total lysates but not in biotinylated (surface) fractions.

claim: AIM-100 induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT or untagged DAT stably expressed in HeLa, HEK293 and human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells.
source: AIM-100 also induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT or untagged DAT stably expressed in HeLa, HEK293 and human neuroblastoma SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Primary cultures of post-natal mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons derived from HA-DAT knock-in mouse displayed strong endocytosis of HA-DAT following AIM-100 treatment.
source: Moreover, primary cultures of post-natal mesencephalic dopaminergic neurons derived from HA-DAT knock-in mouse displayed strong endocytosis of HA-DAT following AIM-100 treatment, as revealed using the HA11 antibody uptake assay (Figure 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by antibody uptake assay in primary neurons shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Cy3-enriched vesicles (internalized HA11:HA-DAT complexes) were abundant in axonal processes, varicosities, axonal widenings and soma of AIM-100-exposed neurons.
source: Cy3-enriched vesicles (internalized HA11:HA-DAT complexes) were abundant in axonal processes, varicosities, axonal widenings and soma of AIM-100-exposed neurons decorated with Cy5 (cell-surface HA11:HA-DAT complexes) (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Observed in microscopy images in Figure 2A-B.

claim: The Cy3/Cy5 ratio (the extent of endocytosis) was several times higher in AIM-100-treated than in control neurons.
source: The Cy3/Cy5 ratio (the extent of endocytosis) was several times higher in AIM-100-treated than in control neurons (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantified from imaging data in Figure 2C.

claim: AIM-100 treatment of striatal synaptosomes prepared from adult HA-DAT mice substantially increased HA-DAT oligomerization.
source: Finally, AIM-100 treatment of striatal synaptosomes prepared from adult HA-DAT mice substantially increased HA-DAT oligomerization (Figure 2D).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of synaptosomes in Figure 2D.

claim: Treatment of PAE/YFP-HA-DAT cells with AIM-100 resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of diffraction-limited (<200 nm) spots (clusters) of YFP-HA-DAT on the basal cell surface.
source: Treatment of PAE/YFP-HA-DAT cells with AIM-100 resulted in a dramatic increase in the number of diffraction-limited (<200 nm) spots (clusters) of YFP-HA-DAT on the basal cell surface (Figure 3A–B, and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Observed by TIR-FM imaging in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The number of YFP-HA-DAT spots approached a maximum after ~10–20 min of AIM-100 treatment and gradually declined during a subsequent 30 min incubation.
source: The number of spots approached a maximum after ~10–20 min of AIM-100 treatment and gradually declined during a subsequent 30 min incubation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse TIR-FM imaging in Figure 3B.

claim: Approximately 35% of YFP-HA-DAT spots persisted for >1 hr, whereas other spots were quite transient with a life-time of a few minutes, putative of endocytic uptake.
source: Approximately 35% of spots persisted for >1 hr, whereas other spots were quite transient with a life-time of a few minutes, putative of endocytic uptake (Figure 3C).
evidence: Analyzed from kymographs in Figure 3C.

claim: Some YFP-HA-DAT spots were moving laterally within the imaging plane, characteristic of newly-formed endocytic vesicles.
source: We noticed some spots were moving laterally within the imaging plane, characteristic of newly-formed endocytic vesicles.
evidence: Observed in TIR-FM time-lapse imaging.

claim: In addition to clustering in planar regions of the membrane, YFP-HA-DAT either moved away from filopodia or formed clusters within the filopodia.
source: In addition to an almost complete clustering of YFP-HA-DAT in the planar regions of the membrane, the transporter either moved away from filopodia or formed clusters within the filopodia (Figure 3D).
evidence: Observed in high magnification time-lapse images in Figure 3D.

claim: Strong accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT at the cell edges was observed during AIM-100 treatment.
source: Simultaneously, strong accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT at the cell edges was observed (Figure 3A; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Observed in TIR-FM imaging in Figure 3A.

claim: AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT precedes its endocytosis.
source: Given the observed timing of cluster formation on the cell surface (Figure 3B), and the kinetics of DAT accumulation in endosomes (Figure 1C), it would appear that AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT precedes its endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of clustering kinetics (Figure 3B) and endocytosis kinetics (Figure 1C).

claim: The intensity of FRET from CFP to YFP was significantly higher in the plasma membrane clusters and intracellular vesicles in AIM-100-treated cells than in vehicle-treated cells.
source: Using the same method of sensitized FRET measuments in cells co-expressing CFP-DAT and YFP-DAT, we found that the intensity of FRET from CFP to YFP was significantly higher in the plasma membrane clusters and intracellular vesicles in AIM-100-treated cells than this intensity in vehicle-treated cells where FRET was measured in various structures and regions of DAT accumulation, such as filopodia, ruffles and cell-cell contacts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured by FRET microscopy and quantified in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Increased FRET in AIM-100-treated cells is indicative of a higher probability or an increased stability of the interaction between DAT molecules, and/or a closer proximity of multiple DAT molecules.
source: An increased FRET in AIM-100-treated cells is indicative of a higher probability or an increased stability of the interaction between DAT molecules, and/or a closer proximity of multiple DAT molecules, thus demonstrating AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization in living cells.
evidence: Interpreted from FRET measurements based on established FRET principles.

claim: AIM-100 does not induce clustering and endocytosis of GFP-NET and GFP-SERT.
source: In contrast to its effects on DAT, AIM-100 did not induce clustering and endocytosis of GFP-NET and GFP-SERT (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated by live-cell imaging in Figure 4A.

claim: GFP-SERT and GFP-NET were detected on western blots as predominantly monomeric species in the absence or presence of AIM-100.
source: Moreover, GFP-SERT and GFP-NET were detected on western blots as predominantly monomeric species in the absence or presence of AIM-100 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: The specificity of AIM-100 effects on transporter endocytosis correlates with the specific effects of AIM-100 on transporter oligomerization.
source: These data demonstrate that the specificity of AIM-100 effects on transporter endocytosis correlates with the specific effects of AIM-100 on transporter oligomerization.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AIM-100 effects on DAT versus NET/SERT in Figure 4.

claim: Treatment of cells with cocaine (1–10 µM) significantly inhibited AIM-100-enhanced oligomerization, clustering in the plasma membrane and endocytosis of YFP-DAT.
source: We therefore tested the effect of cocaine, a competitive inhibitor of DAT, on AIM-100-stimulated DAT oligomerization and endocytosis. Treatment of cells with cocaine (1–10 µM) significantly inhibited AIM-100-enhanced oligomerization, clustering in the plasma membrane and endocytosis of YFP-DAT in cells treated with AIM-100 (Figure 5A–E).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and biochemical assays in Figure 5A-E.

claim: The effects of AIM-100 on DAT are prevented by the occupancy of S1 and S2 binding sites in the DAT or by the outward-facing (OF) conformation of DAT which is stabilized by cocaine binding.
source: These data suggest that the effects of AIM-100 on DAT are prevented by the occupancy of S1 and S2 binding sites in the DAT or by the outward-facing (OF) conformation of DAT which is stabilized by cocaine binding (Loland et al., 2002; Reith et al., 2001).
evidence: Inferred from cocaine inhibition data and cited literature on cocaine's effects on DAT conformation.

claim: W63 is essential for maintaining the network of intramolecular interactions supporting the OF conformation of DAT.
source: W63 is essential for maintaining the network of intramolecular interactions supporting the OF conformation of DAT (Penmatsa et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from previous structural studies.

claim: The W63A mutation results in narrowing the extracellular vestibule, which leads to the loss of substrate transport and cocaine binding, and a higher probability of an inward-facing (IF) conformation.
source: Therefore, the W63A mutation results in narrowing the extracellular vestibule, which leads to the loss of substrate transport and cocaine binding, and a higher probability of an inward-facing (IF) conformation (Chen et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2017; Sorkina et al., 2009).
evidence: Cited from previous functional studies of the W63A mutant.

claim: AIM-100 triggered the robust oligomerization and endocytosis of the W63A mutant but in this case endocytosis was unaffected by cocaine.
source: AIM-100 triggered the robust oligomerization and endocytosis of the W63A mutant but in this case endocytosis was unaffected by cocaine (Figure 5F–H).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and biochemical assays in Figure 5F-H.

claim: The AIM-100 effects on DAT do not require accessible extracellular substrate binding sites per se.
source: These observations imply that (i) the AIM-100 effects on DAT do not require accessible extracellular substrate binding sites per se; but that (ii) cocaine binding to these sites in the wild-type DAT is necessary for counteracting the effects of AIM-100 on DAT.
evidence: Inferred from W63A mutant data showing AIM-100 effects despite inaccessible binding sites.

claim: Cocaine binding to substrate binding sites in the wild-type DAT is necessary for counteracting the effects of AIM-100 on DAT.
source: These observations imply that (i) the AIM-100 effects on DAT do not require accessible extracellular substrate binding sites per se; but that (ii) cocaine binding to these sites in the wild-type DAT is necessary for counteracting the effects of AIM-100 on DAT.
evidence: Inferred from cocaine inhibition of AIM-100 effects in wild-type but not W63A mutant.

claim: Oligomerization and endocytosis of DAT in AIM-100-treated cells were significantly decreased by saturating concentrations (20–100 µM) of DAT substrates, dopamine (DA) and amphetamine (Amph).
source: We found that oligomerization and endocytosis of DAT in AIM-100-treated cells were significantly decreased by saturating concentrations (20–100 µM) of DAT substrates, dopamine (DA) and amphetamine (Amph) (Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and biochemical assays in Figure 6.

claim: Modafinil, an atypical DAT inhibitor, significantly reduced AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization and endocytosis.
source: Moreover, modafinil, an atypical DAT inhibitor, that has been proposed to bind to S1 and S2 sites with micromolar affinity and stabilize DAT in the OC and/or IF states (Schmitt and Reith, 2011), also significantly reduced AIM-100-induced DAT oligomerization and endocytosis (Figure 6).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and biochemical assays in Figure 6.

claim: The occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT.
source: These experiments provide additional evidence that the occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT and suggest that the shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
evidence: Inferred from substrate and inhibitor effects shown in Figures 5-6.

claim: The shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
source: These experiments provide additional evidence that the occupancy of substrate binding sites in wild-type DAT is inhibitory to the AIM-100 effects on DAT and suggest that the shift to an OC/IF conformation is not sufficient for AIM-100 induced oligomerization and endocytosis of the wild-type DAT when substrates or inhibitors are present.
evidence: Inferred from modafinil effects which stabilize OC/IF states but still inhibit AIM-100 effects.

claim: AIM-100 (20 µM) consistently and statistically significantly decreased the Bmax value (an average decrease of 26%) but did not significantly affect KD values of [3-H]CFT binding to DAT.
source: In five independent experiments AIM-100 (20 µM) consistently and statistically significantly decreased the Bmax value (an average decrease of 26%) but did not significantly affect KD values (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Measured in radioligand binding assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The effect of AIM-100 on CFT binding parameters is consistent with the hypothesis that this effect involves an allosteric mechanism.
source: Thus, the effect of AIM-100 on CFT binding parameters is consistent with the hypothesis that this effect involves an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from non-competitive binding pattern (decreased Bmax without affecting KD).

claim: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes.
source: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes, but not with Rab11 (Figure 7A), suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
evidence: Demonstrated by colocalization imaging in Figure 7A-B.

claim: YFP-HA-DAT was not co-localized with Rab11 in AIM-100-treated cells, suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
source: In AIM-100-treated cells YFP-HA-DAT was highly co-localized with Rab5 and EEA.1, markers of early and sorting endosomes, but not with Rab11 (Figure 7A), suggesting that DAT is not efficiently sorted to the recycling compartment.
evidence: Demonstrated by lack of colocalization with Rab11 in Figure 7A.

claim: Only a minimal amount of YFP-HA-DAT was detected in Rab7- and LysoTrackerRed-labeled compartments, indicating that DAT is not sorted to late endosomes and lysosomes after AIM-100-induced internalization.
source: Only a minimal amount of YFP-HA-DAT was detected in Rab7- and LysoTrackerRed-labeled compartments, indicating that DAT is not sorted to late endosomes and lysosomes after AIM-100-induced internalization (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by minimal colocalization in Figure 8A.

claim: AIM-100 did not induce degradation of YFP-HA-DAT or YFP-DAT in contrast to a substantial PKC-dependent degradation of the transporter in cells treated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA).
source: AIM-100 did not induce degradation of YFP-HA-DAT or YFP-DAT in contrast to a substantial PKC-dependent degradation of the transporter in cells treated with phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA) (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: Demonstrated by cycloheximide chase experiments in Figure 8B-C.

claim: AIM-100 does not significantly increase YFP-HA-DAT ubiquitination.
source: This result is consistent with the observation that AIM-100 does not significantly increase YFP-HA-DAT ubiquitination (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation and ubiquitin blotting in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: YFP-HA-DAT labeled with HA11 and internalized in the presence of AIM-100 for 1.5 hr followed by 1.5 hr chase incubation without AIM-100 did not re-distribute from endosomes to the cell surface (recycling).
source: To test this hypothesis, YFP-HA-DAT was labeled with HA11 and internalized in the presence of AIM-100 for 1.5 hr followed by washing and further incubating the cells at 37°C without AIM-100. This 1.5 hr chase incubation did not lead to re-distribution of YFP-HA-DAT from endosomes to the cell surface (recycling), but unexpectedly, actually resulted in an augmented accumulation of YFP-HA-DAT in endosomes (Figure 9).
evidence: Demonstrated by antibody uptake and chase experiments in Figure 9.

claim: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation after AIM-100 treatment.
source: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation (Figure 9), suggesting that cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
evidence: Demonstrated by chase experiments with cocaine in Figure 9.

claim: Cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
source: Cocaine did not prevent additional endocytosis of HA11:YFP-HA-DAT complexes during the chase incubation (Figure 9), suggesting that cocaine binding must precede AIM-100 treatment in order for cocaine to inhibit AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from timing-dependent effects of cocaine shown in Figure 9.

claim: AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible.
source: Importantly, these data indicate that AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible, and that DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
evidence: Inferred from lack of recycling during chase incubation shown in Figure 9.

claim: DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
source: Importantly, these data indicate that AIM-100 has effects on DAT that are not readily reversible, and that DAT internalized in the presence of AIM-100 is not measurably recycled.
evidence: Demonstrated by lack of surface redistribution during chase in Figure 9.

claim: AIM-100 did not inhibit recycling of DAT that had been internalized upon PKC activation and protected from AIM-100-induced endocytosis by cocaine.
source: In contrast, AIM-100 did not inhibit recycling of DAT that had been internalized upon PKC activation and protected from AIM-100-induced endocytosis by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by PMA/cocaine/AIM-100 experiments in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: AIM-100 does not affect the recycling process per se but acts in a cargo-specific fashion by blocking recycling of DAT exclusively only if DAT internalization is induced by AIM-100.
source: These data suggest that AIM-100 does not affect the recycling process per se but acts in a cargo-specific fashion by blocking recycling of DAT exclusively only if DAT internalization is induced by AIM-100.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects on PMA-induced versus AIM-100-induced internalized DAT.

claim: The robust AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is at least partially due to an inability of DAT to recycle in the presence of AIM-100.
source: The data in Figure 9 together with the observations of (i) linear kinetics of DAT accumulation in endosomes (Figure 1C); and (ii) lack of DAT in Rab11 recycling endosomes (Figure 7) suggest that the robust AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is at least partially due to an inability of DAT to recycle in the presence of AIM-100.
evidence: Inferred from combination of recycling, kinetics, and localization data.

claim: The extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100.
source: However, the extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was found to be significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100, and the monensin-dependent accumulation was not inhibited by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by comparison experiments in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: Monensin-dependent accumulation of DAT was not inhibited by cocaine.
source: However, the extent of endosomal accumulation of DAT due to its constitutive internalization in the presence of monensin was found to be significantly smaller than in the presence of AIM-100, and the monensin-dependent accumulation was not inhibited by cocaine (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 9—figure supplement 2.

claim: AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is the result of a combination of an ineffective recycling and an accelerated endocytosis, which is regulated by the mechanism apparently different from that of the constitutive endocytosis revealed in the presence of monensin.
source: Therefore, AIM-100-induced accumulation of DAT in endosomes is the result of a combination of an ineffective recycling and an accelerated endocytosis, which is regulated by the mechanism apparently different from that of the constitutive endocytosis revealed in the presence of monensin.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AIM-100 and monensin effects.

claim: siRNA knock-down of Ack1 (65–80% depletion) did not lead to YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis or other visible changes in the pattern of YFP-HA-DAT localization when compared with the control cells.
source: siRNA knock-down of Ack1 (65–80% depletion, Figure 10A) did not lead to YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis or other visible changes in the pattern of YFP-HA-DAT localization when compared with the control cells (Figure 10B).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging of Ack1-depleted cells in Figure 10A-B.

claim: AIM-100 caused robust YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis in Ack1-depleted cells.
source: Furthermore, AIM-100 caused robust YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis in Ack1-depleted cells (Figure 10C) as evident by the strong increase in YFP-HA-DAT co-localization with Tfn-TxR in endosomes (Figure 10D).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and colocalization analysis in Figure 10C-D.

claim: KRCA-0008, a highly efficient inhibitor of Ack1 (IC50 = 18 nM), did not induce YFP-HA-DAT oligomerization and endocytosis at concentrations of 2–20 µM.
source: Finally, another highly efficient inhibitor of Ack1 (KRCA-0008, IC50 = 18 nM) (Park et al., 2013) did not induce YFP-HA-DAT oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2A) and endocytosis at concentrations of 2–20 µM (Figure 10F).
evidence: Demonstrated by imaging and Western blot in Figure 10F and Figure 10—figure supplement 2A.

claim: AIM-100 induced DAT endocytosis is Ack1-independent in PAE cells.
source: Thus, together the data in Figure 10 indicate that AIM-100 induced DAT endocytosis is Ack1-independent in PAE cells.
evidence: Inferred from Ack1 knockdown and KRCA-0008 experiments in Figure 10.

claim: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis and oligomerization.
source: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis (Figure 10A–C) and oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B), whereas Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited as would be expected (Figure 10B, insets; and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by CHC knockdown experiments in Figure 10A-C and Figure 10—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited by CHC knockdown.
source: Knock-down of clathrin heavy chain (CHC) had no inhibitory effect on AIM-100 induced YFP-HA-DAT endocytosis (Figure 10A–C) and oligomerization (Figure 10—figure supplement 2B), whereas Tfn-TxR endocytosis was strongly inhibited as would be expected (Figure 10B, insets; and Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10B insets and Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: CHC knockdown caused a partial inhibition of the constitutive endocytosis of DAT observed in the presence of monensin.
source: On the other hand, CHC knockdown caused a partial inhibition of the constitutive endocytosis of DAT observed in the presence of monensin (Figure 10—figure supplement 3) [also see (Sorkina et al., 2005)].
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10—figure supplement 3.

claim: AIM-100 re-directs DAT to a specific endocytosis pathway rather than abolishing the plasma membrane retention of DAT.
source: These data suggest that AIM-100 re-directs DAT to a specific endocytosis pathway rather than abolishing the plasma membrane retention of DAT.
evidence: Inferred from differential effects of CHC knockdown on AIM-100-induced versus constitutive endocytosis.

claim: AIM-100-induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT was not significantly inhibited by dynamin-2 siRNA knock-down.
source: Surprisingly, AIM-100-induced endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT was not significantly inhibited by dynamin-2 siRNA knock-down (Figure 11A) and overexpression of the K44A dominant-negative dynamin mutant (data not shown).
evidence: Demonstrated by dynamin-2 knockdown experiments in Figure 11A.

claim: Latranculin B (inhibitor of cortical actin cytoskeleton), ML141 (cdc42 inhibitor) and nystatin (cholesterol-chelating drug) did not affect AIM-100-dependent DAT endocytosis.
source: Latranculin B (inhibitor of cortical actin cytoskeleton), ML141 (cdc42 inhibitor) and nystatin (cholesterol-chelating drug) also did not affect AIM-100-dependent DAT endocytosis (Figure 11B).
evidence: Demonstrated by pharmacological inhibitor experiments in Figure 11B.

claim: The PKC inhibitor, Go6976, did not block AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
source: Further, the PKC inhibitor, Go6976, did not block AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 10—figure supplement 1 (likely referring to Figure 9—figure supplement 1).

claim: ML141 treatment induced a moderate endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT, suggesting that cdc42 could be involved in DAT retention at the cell surface.
source: ML141 treatment induced a moderate endocytosis of YFP-HA-DAT (Figure 11B), suggesting that cdc42 could be involved in DAT retention at the cell surface.
evidence: Observed in Figure 11B and inferred from the effect of cdc42 inhibition.

claim: An inhibitor of phospholipase D, FIPI reduced AIM-100-induced endocytosis two-fold.
source: Interestingly, an inhibitor of phospholipase D, FIPI reduced AIM-100-induced endocytosis two-fold.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 11B.

claim: The involvement of phospholipase D may be attributed to the importance of the product of phospholipase D activity, phosphatidic acid, in membrane fission and fusion processes.
source: The involvement of phospholipase D may be attributed to the importance of the product of phospholipase D activity, phosphatidic acid, in membrane fission and fusion processes (Donaldson, 2009).
evidence: Inferred from known functions of phosphatidic acid cited from literature.

claim: Src kinase family inhibitor, PP2, and genistein, a wide-range tyrosine kinase inhibitor, did not alter the subcellular distribution of YFP-HA-DAT in untreated or AIM-100-treated PAE cells.
source: Src kinase family inhibitor, PP2, and genistein, a wide-range tyrosine kinase inhibitor, did not alter the subcellular distribution of YFP-HA-DAT in untreated or AIM-100-treated PAE cells (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as experimental observation without shown data.

claim: AIM-100 induces DAT endocytosis via a novel CIE mechanism that does not involve caveolae-, CLIC/GEEC-, Arf6-, Rho-family-GTPase- and endophilin-dependent pathways, as well as micropinocytosis.
source: These experiments ruled out the involvement of many known CIE mechanisms, such as those underlying caveolae-, CLIC/GEEC-, Arf6-, Rho-family-GTPase- and endophilin-dependent pathways, as well as micropinocytosis (Boucrot et al., 2015; Mayor et al., 2014). Thus, collectively the data in Figures 10 and 11 suggest that AIM-100 induces DAT endocytosis via a novel CIE mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from negative results with multiple pathway inhibitors and cited literature on CIE mechanisms.

claim: DAT is responsible for the clearance of dopamine released from synapses, and therefore, controls the duration and amplitude of dopamine signaling in the brain.
source: DAT is responsible for the clearance of dopamine released from synapses, and therefore, controls the duration and amplitude of dopamine signaling in the brain (Giros et al., 1991; Jaber et al., 1997; Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from established literature on DAT function.

claim: DAT is the principal target of psychostimulants like cocaine and amphetamines.
source: DAT is also known to be the principal target of psychostimulants like cocaine and amphetamines (Gainetdinov and Caron, 2003; Gowrishankar et al., 2014; Spiga et al., 2008; Volkow and Morales, 2015; Willuhn et al., 2010; Wise, 2008).
evidence: Cited from established literature on psychostimulant pharmacology.

claim: DAT belongs to the high-affinity saline carrier (SLC) six gene family of Na+, Cl--dependent transporters consisting of 12 TM domains, and cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails.
source: DAT belongs to the high-affinity saline carrier (SLC) six gene family of Na+, Cl--dependent transporters consisting of 12 TM domains, and cytosolic N- and C-terminal tails (Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from established structural knowledge of DAT.

claim: DAT is proposed to form dimers and high-order oligomers, although the mechanisms of oligomerization are not understood.
source: DAT is proposed to form dimers and high-order oligomers, although the mechanisms of oligomerization are not understood (Hastrup et al., 2001; Hastrup et al., 2003; Li et al., 2010; Sorkina et al., 2003; Torres et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on DAT oligomerization.

claim: DAT dimerization/multimerization modulates the substrate transport activity of DAT and is necessary for the effective transport of newly-synthesized DAT from the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: It has been proposed that DAT dimerization/multimerization modulates the substrate transport activity of DAT and is necessary for the effective transport of newly-synthesized DAT from the endoplasmic reticulum (Chen and Reith, 2008; Sorkina et al., 2003; Torres et al., 2003; Zhen et al., 2015; Zhen and Reith, 2018).
evidence: Cited from previous functional studies of DAT oligomerization.

claim: DAT has been shown to internalize in response to protein kinase C (PKC) activation, amphetamines, substrates, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, neuronal activity and inhibition of Ack1.
source: DAT has been shown to internalize in response to protein kinase C (PKC) activation, amphetamines, substrates, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, neuronal activity and inhibition of Ack1 (Activated Cdc42 Kinase) (Eriksen et al., 2009; Gabriel et al., 2013; Hoover et al., 2007; Huff et al., 1997; Melikian and Buckley, 1999; Rao et al., 2012; Richardson et al., 2016; Sorkina et al., 2003; Vaughan et al., 1997; Wheeler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from multiple previous studies on DAT endocytosis regulation.

claim: DAT appears to be capable of internalization through both CME and CIE.
source: DAT appears to be capable of internalization through both CME and CIE (Cremona et al., 2011; Gabriel et al., 2013; Sorkina et al., 2013; Sorkina et al., 2005; Wheeler et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on DAT endocytosis mechanisms.

claim: The strong effect of AIM-100 on DAT oligomerization is the first example of a chemically-enhanced non-covalent oligomerization of a multi-spanning TM protein.
source: To our knowledge, the strong effect of AIM-100 on DAT oligomerization is the first example of a chemically-enhanced non-covalent oligomerization of a multi-spanning TM protein.
evidence: Stated as a novel finding based on authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: The bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer.
source: Whereas the bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer (Yamashita et al., 2005), Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer (Penmatsa et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from structural biology literature.

claim: Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer.
source: Whereas the bacterial homolog of DAT LeuT was crystalized as a dimer (Yamashita et al., 2005), Drosophila DAT was crystallized as a monomer (Penmatsa et al., 2013).
evidence: Cited from structural biology literature.

claim: The 'minimal' DAT oligomer detected at ~290 kDa for YFP-HA-DAT and ~190 kDa for HA-DAT may correspond to a trimer.
source: Detection of a 290 kDa species of YFP-DAT/YFP-HA-DAT (Figures 1, 4, 5, 6 and 8 and supplements) and a 190 kDa species of HA-DAT (Figure 2D) suggests that this 'minimal' DAT oligomer may correspond to a trimer.
evidence: Inferred from molecular weight calculations based on Western blot data.

claim: Chemical cross-linking of Cys246 and Cys306 results in the formation of dimers, trimers and tetramers of DAT.
source: Although DAT and other SLC6 transporters are typically thought to be dimers, it was reported that chemical cross-linking of Cys246 and Cys306 results in the formation of dimers, trimers and tetramers of DAT (Hastrup et al., 2001; Hastrup et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from previous cross-linking studies.

claim: Despite the structural similarity of catecholamine transporters, their oligomerization mechanisms might be fundamentally different.
source: The fact that similar SDS-resistant oligomeric species of NET and SERT were not detected in the absence or presence of AIM-100 implies that despite the structural similarity of catecholamine transporters and contrary to a generally accepted notion of an equivalence in their oligomerization mechanisms (Alguel et al., 2016), these mechanisms might actually be fundamentally different.
evidence: Inferred from differential oligomerization responses to AIM-100 among DAT, NET, and SERT.

claim: An interaction of SERT with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) is important for the formation of stable oligomers of SERT.
source: For example, an interaction of SERT with phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) was recently demonstrated to be important for the formation of stable oligomers of SERT (Anderluh et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from recent SERT oligomerization study.

claim: The PIP2-dependent oligomerization mechanism may not be involved in DAT oligomerization.
source: However, this mechanism may not be involved in DAT oligomerization. DAT has been shown to be oligomeric in endosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum (Sorkina et al., 2003; Zhen and Reith, 2018), where PIP2 is present at extremely low levels (Hammond and Balla, 2015).
evidence: Inferred from DAT oligomerization in compartments lacking PIP2.

claim: Differences in the sites of PIP2 binding to DAT and SERT (amino-terminus versus transmembrane core, respectively) may be responsible for different mechanisms of their oligomerization.
source: It is possible that differences in the sites of PIP2 binding to DAT and SERT (amino-terminus versus transmembrane core, respectively) (Buchmayer et al., 2013; Hamilton et al., 2014) are responsible for different mechanisms of their oligomerization.
evidence: Speculated based on cited differences in PIP2 binding sites.

claim: Formation of highly stable oligomers and DAT clustering in living cells correlated with DAT endocytosis in experiments that examined the effects of transporter inhibitors and substrates, and compared AIM-100 effects on three monoamine transporters.
source: Formation of highly stable oligomers and DAT clustering in living cells correlated with DAT endocytosis in experiments that examined the effects of transporter inhibitors and substrates, and compared AIM-100 effects on three monoamine transporters (Figures 4–6).
evidence: Observed correlation across multiple experimental conditions in Figures 4-6.

claim: The fast kinetics of AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT suggests that DAT oligomerization and clustering are part of the mechanism mediating AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
source: These observations together with the fast kinetics of AIM-100-induced clustering of DAT (Figure 3B–C) suggest that DAT oligomerization and clustering are part of the mechanism mediating AIM-100-induced DAT endocytosis.
evidence: Inferred from temporal relationship between clustering and endocytosis.

claim: The dramatic accumulation of DAT in endosomes following AIM-100 treatment is a synergistic effect due to both accelerated endocytosis and inefficient recycling.
source: Several lines of evidence suggest that such a dramatic accumulation is a synergistic effect due to both accelerated endocytosis and inefficient recycling (Figures 7–9).
evidence: Inferred from combined data on endocytosis kinetics, localization, and recycling experiments.

claim: In early endosomes DAT oligomers are not efficiently packaged into tubular recycling carriers due to the large size of these oligomers.
source: We propose that in early endosomes DAT oligomers are not efficiently packaged into tubular recycling carriers due to the large size of these oligomers.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on oligomer size and recycling data.

claim: When monomeric receptors that normally recycle are crosslinked by multivalent ligands, these receptors are partially mis-targeted to the lysosomal pathway.
source: When monomeric receptors that normally recycle are crosslinked by multivalent ligands, these receptors have been shown to be partially mis-targeted to the lysosomal pathway (Geuze et al., 1987; Hopkins and Trowbridge, 1983).
evidence: Cited from previous studies on receptor trafficking.

claim: Targeting of non-ubiquitinated cargo to lysosomes may occur on a substantially longer time scale than 2 hr.
source: It is possible that targeting of non-ubiquitinated cargo to lysosomes occurs on a substantially longer time scale than our 2 hr time-course experiments (Tewari et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculated based on cited literature on lysosomal targeting kinetics.

claim: The pathways and mechanisms of DAT endocytosis in the presence of AIM-100 observed by Wu and co-workers and in the present study may be different.
source: This raises a question of whether the pathways and mechanisms of DAT endocytosis in the presence of AIM-100 observed by Wu and co-workers (Wu et al., 2015) and in the present study are different.
evidence: Questioned based on differences in clathrin and cdc42 dependence between studies.

claim: Considerable general toxicity of pitstop-2 has been reported.
source: However, considerable general toxicity of this compound has been reported (Lemmon and Traub, 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Willox et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from literature on pitstop-2 toxicity.

claim: Pitstop-2 has been shown to strongly block CIE.
source: Pitstop-2 has also been shown to strongly block the CIE (Dutta et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from literature on pitstop-2 effects.

claim: Although Ack1 was reported to be associated with the clathrin coated structures, the importance of Ack1 for CME has not been established.
source: Furthermore, although Ack1 was reported to be associated with the clathrin coated structures, the importance of Ack1 for CME has not been established (Shen et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from literature on Ack1 localization and function.

claim: Screening for kinases involved in DAT regulation did not reveal the involvement of Ack1.
source: Finally, it should be noted that screening for kinases involved in DAT regulation did not reveal the involvement of Ack1 (Vuorenpää et al., 2016a).
evidence: Cited from kinase screening study.

claim: AIM-100 increases DAT oligomerization by directly interacting with DAT in its conformation favorable for oligomerization and thus stabilizing DAT trimers/oligomers.
source: First, we propose that AIM-100 increases DAT oligomerization by directly interacting with DAT in its conformation favorable for oligomerization and thus stabilizing DAT trimers/oligomers.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: The AIM-100:DAT interaction and the occupancy of the substrate binding sites are mutually exclusive.
source: We also suggest that the AIM-100:DAT interaction and the occupancy of the substrate binding sites are mutually exclusive.
evidence: Proposed based on inhibitor/substrate competition data.

claim: DAT oligomerization results in extensive surface clustering, which may be driven by the hydrophobic mismatch of oligomers and the membrane.
source: Second, we propose that DAT oligomerization results in an extensive surface clustering, which may be driven by the hydrophobic mismatch of oligomers and the membrane.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on biophysical principles.

claim: Clustering is typically observed as the consequence of ligand-induced dimerization of receptors.
source: Clustering is typically observed as the consequence of ligand-induced dimerization of receptors [for example (Zidovetzki et al., 1981; Zidovetzki et al., 1986).
evidence: Cited from literature on receptor clustering.

claim: DAT clusters may stabilize or promote spontaneous membrane invagination and scission leading to a coat-independent endocytosis.
source: Third, DAT clusters may stabilize or promote spontaneous membrane invagination and scission leading to a coat-independent endocytosis.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: TM cargo-induced membrane remodeling has been proposed.
source: Such TM cargo-induced membrane remodeling has been proposed (Johannes and Mayor, 2010; Johannes et al., 2014), although experimentally-proven examples in intact cells or in vitro are rare (Callenberg et al., 2012; Davies et al., 2012; Rosholm et al., 2017; Spoden et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from literature on cargo-induced membrane remodeling.

claim: Independence of the AIM-100-induced endocytosis of clathrin, dynamin and other mechanisms mediating various known CIE pathways supports the hypothesis that this endocytosis may not involve a specific membrane bending/scission machinery.
source: Independence of the AIM-100-induced endocytosis of clathrin, dynamin and other mechanisms mediating various known CIE pathways, supports the hypothesis that this endocytosis may not involve a specific membrane bending/scission machinery.
evidence: Inferred from negative results with multiple pathway inhibitors.

claim: Coat-free endocytosis may serve as part of the regulatory and quality-control mechanisms that remove excess DAT from the cell surface in the absence of extracellular substrates and may clear DAT oligomers as they are functionally impaired.
source: Our findings inevitably lead to a hypothesis that coat-free endocytosis may serve as part of the regulatory and quality-control mechanisms that remove excess DAT from the cell surface in the absence of extracellular substrates and may clear DAT oligomers as they are functionally impaired (Zhen and Reith, 2018).
evidence: Hypothesized based on findings and cited literature on DAT oligomer function.
